description_full: J.B. Hunt Transport Services, Inc. provides surface transportation, delivery, and logistic services in the United States. It operates through five segments: Intermodal, Dedicated Contract Services, Integrated Capacity Solutions, Final Mile Services, and Truckload. The JBI segment offers intermodal freight solutions. It operates 124,838 pieces of company-owned trailing equipment; owns and maintains its chassis fleet of 104,474 units; and manages a fleet of 5,880 company-owned tractors, 308 independent contractor trucks, and 8,704 company drivers. The DCS segment designs, develops, and executes supply chain solutions that support various transportation networks. As of December 31, 2025, it operated 11,878 company-owned trucks, 761 customer-owned trucks, and a contractor trucks. It operates 26,767 owned pieces of trailing equipment and 5,218 customer-owned trailers. The ICS segment provides freight brokerage and transportation logistics solutions; flatbed, refrigerated, expedited, and less-than-truckload, as well as dry-van and intermodal solutions; online multimodal marketplace; and logistics management services for customers to outsource their transportation functions. The FMS segment delivers services through 1,085 company-owned trucks, 169 customer-owned trucks, and 39 independent contractor trucks; and 1,091 owned pieces of trailing equipment and 98 customer-owned trailers. The JBT segment provides dry-van freight services by utilizing tractors and trailers operating over roads and highways through two company-owned tractors and 12,658 company-owned trailers. It transports or arranges for the transportation of freight, such as general merchandise, specialty consumer items, appliances, home furnishings, forest, paper, rubber, plastic products, food, beverages, building materials, apparel, accessories, soaps, cosmetics, automotive parts, agricultural products, electronics, and chemicals. The company was incorporated in 1961 and is headquartered in Lowell, Arkansas.

financial_summary: J.B. Hunt Transport Services, I is a large-cap industrials business with a $20.3B market cap on $12.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 9% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $948M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.81× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -13.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 11.5×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 21% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.65x).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 35% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 18% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $216.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 29% in the 2022 bear market and 53% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $197 (margin of safety -11%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $129 to $301 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 30.7 vs 23.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 43% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $280 on average, 28% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 8.9%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.21).
It converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.81x, but high accruals (-13.6% of assets).
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($17.3M of cash against $1.5B of debt), with interest covered 11.5x.
The current ratio of 0.83 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -6.8% over 3 years, 4.5% over 5 years and 6.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.8% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 6.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.5% on average.
own: Insiders own 20.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 80%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $4.2M sold).
It returns 5.4% a year to shareholders (4.6% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 8.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 31,750 employees, each generates about $378K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 8.0% a year.
That works out to $30K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
